metadata.description: Persuasive message treatments for each policy issue (both 'in favor' and 'against' versions)

policies.label: Allow religious denial of service
policies.text: Allow businesses to deny service to a customer if the request conflicts with the owner's religious beliefs
policies.message_in_favor: The policy would help protect religious minorities in the U.S. from discrimination and persecution. For example, imagine that a customer asked a Muslim baker to make a food item that deliberately mocked and degraded their religious culture. This policy would allow them some protection in refusing to serve the customer. This is sensible policy: we shouldn't force religious minorities to engage in behaviors that degrade and demean them — that isn't what America is about. Yes, religion should be separate from government, but in the private sector minorities should not be forced to do whatever their customers ask. That is capitalism gone mad. What's more, there is a natural guard against abuse of this policy: if businesses deny service to too many customers, they will go bust. Therefore, the policy would not be abused. It mostly just provides religious minorities the option to protect themselves from being deliberately degraded and humiliated.
policies.message_against: The personal biases of business owners should not be allowed to disrupt a fair and profitable business transaction in a free market principle. This well. In addition, this policy could be abused and lead to discrimination. For example, under this policy, a fundamentalist Muslim shop owner could legally refuse service to a woman. This goes directly against American values. Business owners could also pretend to refuse service for a religious reason, when really they are just prejudiced against the customer for other reasons. Ultimately, businesses are entities that exist in the public marketplace and should respect the dignity and rights of all customers, especially in America where unacceptable.

policies.label: Subsidized healthcare for immigrants
policies.text: Provide illegal immigrants with access to government-subsidized healthcare
policies.message_in_favor: In the long-run this policy would reduce healthcare costs for everyone in America. The reason is simple: by making it easier for illegal immigrants to receive healthcare, their minor health issues would not develop into serious conditions later. Treating these serious conditions is a greater drain on the finances of U.S. healthcare than treating minor issues early. Therefore, healthcare centers would not have to increase the prices of their services to compensate for the costs of treating serious conditions. Ultimately, this would save the U.S. government and all American citizens money on healthcare expenses. This policy is just commonsense.
policies.message_against: This policy could slow or prevent the expanding of health coverage to struggling American citizens. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that about 31 million Americans are uninsured. Therefore, providing health coverage to an additional 6 million undocumented immigrants, many of which would not pay into it because they work 'off the books,' would drain financial resources that could have been used to expand access to many struggling American citizens. This is why liberal democracies with universal, government-run healthcare — like Norway — place tough restrictions on healthcare for undocumented immigrants; they can get emergency care, but are required to pay other costs.

policies.label: Abolish electoral college
policies.text: Abolish the electoral college
policies.message_in_favor: The electoral college ignores the will of the American people because it makes it possible to win a presidential election without the majority of voters. For example, in theory a president can get enough votes to win an election with just 23% of the vote. This system makes it possible for a minority of the country to rule over the substantial majority. Clearly this goes against core principles of democracy. At the moment, battleground states determine the result of each election, and so candidates must only appeal to a minority of states instead of the whole country. This gives a few states the power to control the entire nation's future. In addition, the electoral college means the votes of Americans in non-battleground states are usually not decisive or even meaningful.
policies.message_against: Without the electoral college, elections would be biased toward states with large populations. For example, over half of the U.S. population lives in just nine states. This could easily sway the result of them if an election if we were to abolish the electoral college. Even more worrying, over 82% of the U.S. population lives in urban areas. This means that candidates would simply campaign in the most population-dense metropolitan areas, ignoring people in rural areas and towns. Therefore, if we were to abolish the electoral college, rural Americans and most smaller states would be largely left out in selecting the president, which may lead to what the Founders warned against, 'tyranny of the majority'. The electoral college is far from perfect, but abolishing it is a bad idea.

policies.label: Allow death penalty
policies.text: Allow the use of the death penalty
policies.message_in_favor: Some crimes are so uniquely brutal that prison is too weak to provide justice for victims and their communities. For example, names currently on death row include Dzhokhar Tsarnaev — the Boston Marathon bomber who murdered or injured nearly 270 innocent people — and Dylann Roof, the Charleston church shooter who murdered nine African Americans in cold blood. These criminals deprived many innocent people of their right to life, by terribly brutal and racist murders. If it were not for the death penalty, these men would instead be in prison, where they could carry on with their own lives in some way: reading books, exercising and even watching selected TV shows. Is this right? Certainly there should be a high standard of proof and a uniquely brutal crime to warrant the death penalty. But banning it completely is wrong: it removes a form of justice which many victims and their communities may need in order to find peace and closure. They deserve that option.
policies.message_against: No human being should be allowed to pass final judgment onto any other human being, especially since many innocent people have been wrongly convicted and sentenced to death in the U.S. Obviously, the justice system will sometimes make mistakes. But the death penalty makes these mistakes permanent because they take away human life. As a result of this, nearly all Western democracies have banned the practice, while oppressive governments — including China, Iran and Saudi Arabia — use it most frequently. In addition, the death penalty is also very costly: more than a dozen U.S. states have found that death penalty cases are up to 10 times more expensive than similar non-death penalty cases. Where does this extra money come from? Taxes, of course. The government could cut taxes on American citizens.

policies.label: Require women on boards
policies.text: Make it a requirement for businesses to have women on their board of directors
policies.message_in_favor: The main goal of a business is to maximize profits, and research suggests that more diverse teams can improve business profitability. For example, in 2019 world-leading consulting firm McKinsey analyzed the performance of 1,000 companies from 15 different countries. They found that companies with the greatest gender diversity were more likely to have above-average profitability than companies with the lowest gender diversity. This result makes sense: by bringing different perspectives to problems, diversity can prevent teams from being stuck in one lane of unproductive thought for too long. Rapid problem-solving is essential to being a successful business. In order to maintain America's economic advantage over high-growth countries like China, U.S. businesses must put ideology aside and embrace strategies that are shown to work.
policies.message_against: Under this policy, women who are included on the board of directors may be seen as underqualified, since their presence is required by the government. This would hurt women everywhere. For example, many colleagues would likely perceive the requirement as unfair, believing that the best person for the job should get the job — irrespective of gender. The policy could therefore reinforce implicit biases that women everywhere are harming that could overcome. There is also evidence that the policy is ineffective, leaving most women behind. Research in Norway shows that despite founder-representative imbalances being implemented for top executive positions, female under-representation and gender wage disparities persisted at all other levels. We need effective policy to combat gender bias, and forcing women on their board of directors does not seem like an effective strategy.

policies.label: Amnesty for illegal immigrants
policies.text: Give working illegal immigrants temporary amnesty
policies.message_in_favor: This policy would increase tax revenue for the U.S., because workers who are currently paid 'under the table' would join the open economy. Statistics support this claim: immigrants paid nearly $500 billion in taxes in 2019 and the federal government has spent $333 billion on agencies to carry out immigration enforcement since 2003. These are huge sums of money. Therefore, by giving working illegal immigrants temporary amnesty, the U.S. would become wealthier by boosting tax revenue and reducing spending on immigration enforcement. This would allow the government to lower taxes for working- and middle-class American families, or increase funding for important community initiatives such as crime prevention and affordable housing programs.
policies.message_against: It's often easy for politicians to say we should give illegal immigrants amnesty because in the end these people don't live in their neighborhoods. They are much more likely to live in black and other minority neighborhoods, where they compete for jobs with black and other minority groups. This competition ultimately decreases wages and makes it harder for black and minority American citizens to get a job that pays a living wage — harming their chances at achieving social and economic mobility. A more sensible solution for these communities is to put the matter to a vote and let the American people decide. This solution respects the reality of the situation, and gives the American people — and those communities most affected by immigration — the right to decide what they want by voting for it.

policies.label: Limit donations to candidates
policies.text: Limit the amount of money a candidate can receive from a donor
policies.message_in_favor: Money has corrupted U.S. politics so that it favors elite interests over the interests of American citizens. For example, in the 2016 election cycle the top individual donor gave $90 million; in 2020, it was $215 million. These massive individual donations are made possible by the Citizens United Supreme Court decision in 2010. This decision allows corporations, unions and wealthy individuals to spend unlimited sums of money on ads and other political tools to get their preferred candidate elected. Though the money is not 'donated' to the candidate directly, it has a huge influence in getting them elected. This betrays the average American citizen and the core principles of democracy. A single person can dramatically influence U.S. elections, making the votes of ordinary Americans less important. This policy is a first step toward protecting U.S. democracy and the vote of ordinary Americans.
policies.message_against: Political campaigns are expensive to run, and putting limits on individual donations to one candidate of federal elections cost candidates receiving donations may face difficulties. For example, many organizations that provide candidates enough money to run a campaign. Therefore, limiting individual donations could unfairly favor one candidate over another. For example, the 2020 federal elections cost $14 billion. Although many candidates receive funding from small individual donations, many of them already have connections to organizations that provide enough money to run a campaign. Therefore, limiting individual donations would not hurt these establishment candidates. Instead, it would disadvantage new candidates with fresh ideas who are not already 'in bed' with business and other large-dollar funding organizations. Furthermore, limiting individual donations would not reduce the corrupting influence of big money in U.S. politics: corporations would still be able to donate unlimited sums to get candidates elected. Policy should target corporations, not individuals.

policies.label: More restrictions at U.S. border
policies.text: Increase restrictions on current U.S. border security policy
policies.message_in_favor: Having a secure border is fairer and more humane to immigrants in the long run. For example, tighter border controls would discourage immigrants from paying people smugglers to take them across the U.S. border. These journeys can be perilous for immigrants, because smugglers only care about exploiting people for profit. Research has documented extreme human rights abuses, with smuggled migrants subject to threats, abuse, exploitation and torture, and even death at the hands of smugglers. In addition, many would-be immigrants are patiently waiting in their home countries while their application to come to America is processed. It is extremely unfair to these individuals and their families to make it easy for immigrants to 'cut in line' by illegally crossing the border, effectively taking the place of people who have waited for a long time to go through the legal process. The U.S. should encourage legal immigration, while discouraging illegal immigration and people smuggling by increasing border security.
policies.message_against: Increasing restrictions on border security is a waste of government money, which would be better spent on directly improving the lives of American citizens. For example, estimates of the cost of increasing U.S. border security have been as large as $21 billion. This vast sum of money could instead be spent on community development and employment programs designed to get struggling Americans back to work and to improve their quality of life. What's more, evidence suggests that increased border security may not do much to stop illegal immigration, despite its huge cost. In 2006, the Pew Research Center calculated that more than a third of all unauthorized immigrants entered America lawfully and then simply overstayed their visas. By 2012, visa overstays accounted for more than 50 percent of all new unauthorized immigrants in the U.S. We need smarter policy than simply adding more border restrictions.

policies.label: Require work for Medicaid
policies.text: Make it a requirement that people work in order to receive Medicaid
policies.message_in_favor: This policy would benefit people's health and their communities. The reason is simple: good healthcare is not simply about receiving treatment from a doctor, but also about preventing health issues in the first place. According to Brian Neale, a former director at Medicaid, the policy promotes participation in community-engagement activities — such as working, volunteering, going to school and receiving job training — in return for Medicaid benefits. He points to research showing that unemployment is harmful to people's health, and that activities such as volunteering are associated with improved health outcomes. In addition to these health benefits, the policy can be good for the community. Medicaid costs $560 billion annually, and is mostly funded by the government. This leaves less money for other government-funded community programs. Therefore, requiring people who receive Medicaid to participate in community-engagement activities helps to make up for this loss of spending on community programs.
policies.message_against: This policy is designed to help people on Medicaid get back to work. However, there is powerful evidence that it does not achieve this goal. For example, a 2017 study looked at two groups of people who got aid: those who were required to work and those who were not. Tracking the people for five years, it found that those who had a work requirement and those who had not are just as likely to be working. Sometimes the people without a requirement were even more likely to be working. Importantly, Medicaid itself does not cause people to stop working: a 2018 study concluded that Medicaid expansion has had neutral or even positive effects on employment rates. Medicaid has not led to large numbers of people stopping job searches in order to live off the government. Instead, more people find work. Therefore, while we should of course help people on Medicaid get employment and become more self-reliant, work requirements are not effective.

policies.label: Allow assisted suicide
policies.text: Allow terminally ill patients to end their lives via assisted suicide
policies.message_in_favor: This policy respects patients' autonomy, relieves their suffering, and is safe from abuse. Since patients make their own healthcare decisions throughout life — by determining which medical treatments they will have — they should also have a say in the circumstances of their deaths. For terminal illnesses that cause patients unmanageable suffering, assisted suicide is also humane and compassionate. Importantly, there are many safeguards to prevent abuse of the policy. For example, there is a strict requirement that a patient choosing assisted suicide be informed of all end-of-life options, and that at least two witnesses confirm that the patient is making the request of their own free will. These safeguards remove most of the main concerns about assisted suicide policy. If assisted suicide is not available, patients may try to do it themselves anyway. This is much worse for everyone, especially their loved ones.
policies.message_against: This policy encourages suicide and is a slippery slope. For example, after high-profile assisted suicides, there is often a spike in the number of other people committing suicide. After a high-profile assisted suicide in Oregon in 2014, the number of similar people who ended their lives by the same method more than doubled. Furthermore, both allow assisted suicide (and euthanasia (mercy killing)). Over the years there has been a steady increase in acceptable criteria there. Currently, patients who suffer from depression, dementia or being 'tired of life' may be euthanized. In some cases, minors may also be euthanized. Belgium highlights that vulnerable populations are especially likely among the largest increases in rates granting euthanasia requests were among women and those with less education. These are worrying trends.

policies.label: Illegal to burn U.S. flag
policies.text: Make it illegal to burn the American flag
policies.message_in_favor: Flag burning is intended to intimidate people, not to engage in constructive or liberating speech. It is easy to see why burning the U.S. flag is intimidating: for many Americans, the nation's flag represents its people, and therefore burning the flag represents the destruction of its people. This message does not belong in civilized democracy. Indeed, this is why it is illegal for the KKK to burn a cross in public with the intent to intimidate others. Some people fear that banning flag burning represents censorship. However, it could actually encourage people to express unpopular and minority viewpoints — because a robust system of free speech depends upon a sense of shared community and freedom from intimidation. This is why progressive liberal democracies, such as Germany, restrict flag burning. If people want to protest against the U.S. government, there are many ways to do this that do not involve intimidating others using fire.
policies.message_against: The U.S. flag is symbolic of freedom of expression, among many other values. The flag is therefore a direct contradiction of what it represents. Flag burning is considered offensive because it sends a political message, in much the same way as people who go on strike, march in protest, or use other forms of speech to express their politics. The way to fight political expression with which one disagrees is not to outlaw it, but to express strong disapproval and to use arguments and reason to show why it is wrong. Removing people's fundamental right to freely express themselves in one case makes it easier for the government to restrict other forms of political expression that it deems 'offensive'. This is a slippery slope and directly undermines American values.

policies.label: Deny criminals the vote
policies.text: Deny convicted criminals the right to vote
policies.message_in_favor: This policy makes sense. Domestic terrorists should not have the power to choose leaders for the very country they conspired against; male rapists should not have a say in regulating the very woman's bodily autonomy they violated; and convicted Klansmen and neo-Nazis should not be able to influence the politics of the Black communities they terrorized. Criminals not only commit crimes against their victims, but also against society as a whole. When they break the social contract of society and commit brutal crimes in the process, criminals allow society to restrict some of their freedoms. If society does not trust them to possess firearms or be chosen for a jury, then society should not trust them to decide the direction of the country by voting in elections. This is a real danger: according to a 2002 study, many U.S. elections would have had different outcomes if all felons had had the vote.
policies.message_against: Once felons have served their prison term and re-entered society, they should be allowed to vote because this reduces the chance they will re-offend. Indeed, most felons who cannot vote have already returned to society, having completed their prison term: only about 25 percent of those who cannot vote are currently in prison. It is in society's best interest that ex-felons move on with their lives and do not re-offend. Just as most ex-felons are allowed to have family relations and jobs — both of which make re-offending less likely — they should also be allowed to vote too. Evidence supports this logic: a recent report points out that allowing ex-felons to vote encourages them to see themselves as meaningful participants in society, and to feel invested in its outcome. Both of these factors will make it less likely for them to re-offend. In fact, one study found that Minnesotan ex-felons who voted in 1996 were only half as likely to be re-arrested later compared to those who did not vote.

policies.label: Ban juvenile solitary confinement
policies.text: Ban the use of solitary confinement for juveniles in prison
policies.message_in_favor: While solitary confinement is necessary for some dangerous adult prisoners, it should be banned for juveniles because the harms outweigh the benefits. (Juveniles are people under 18 years of age; they are children). In solitary confinement, children are isolated physically, socially and emotionally — often for many days at a time — at a crucial point in their development. One of the main goals of prison is to rehabilitate people so that they can re-enter society and become productive members of it. This is especially true of children, who will re-enter society at some point because they were imprisoned at a young age. Evidence suggests that solitary confinement can damage the development of children, and this damage can be permanent. This does not help their rehabilitation, and may prevent them ever again contributing positively to society. Therefore, as well as it being morally wrong to put children in solitary confinement, there is also a practical argument against it: it is bad for society in the long run.
policies.message_against: Solitary confinement is already used rarely when the prisoner is a juvenile. For example, between September 2014 and 2015 federal authorities were notified of just 13 juveniles who were put in solitary confinement across America. Those juveniles who do get put in solitary confinement do so for good reasons. For example, because they are too dangerous to be left around other inmates, or because they risk being attacked by other inmates. In either case, for the safety of everybody involved it is important that prisons have the option of temporarily separating some inmates from others. Furthermore, when used rarely and cleverly, solitary confinement can be a powerful motivator to keep young prisoners on the 'straight and narrow,' helping them stay out of trouble. Solitary confinement can and should be used rarely for juveniles, but it is not helpful to completely ban it.

policies.label: Minimum sentences for drugs
policies.text: Allow mandatory minimum prison sentences for people charged with drug possession
policies.message_in_favor: Mandatory minimum sentencing is a necessary and effective deterrent against drug dealing in America. The policy is effective because drug dealing is a crime of 'calculation': people make a conscious decision to buy drugs, carry drugs and sell drugs. This is different from a crime of 'passion,' where somebody sees red and loses control of their behavior. While crimes of passion do not respond to deterrent policies, crimes of calculation do: drug dealers must weigh the potential costs and benefits of their criminal behavior. Mandatory minimum sentences are a clear signal that the costs could be high if they get caught. Therefore, it strongly discourages drug possession. Strong discouragement of drugs crimes is crucial in America because the economic cost of drug abuse is as high as $200 billion. The human cost is countless numbers of ruined lives, broken families and brutal murders. We must be clear that illegal drugs are not tolerated in the U.S.
policies.message_against: Mandatory minimum sentences are a one-size-fits-all response to crimes that are definitely not equal. For example, a mother giving her child CBD to combat seizures would be breaking federal law. And under this policy, she could face time in prison. What parent wouldn't use a non-toxic substance to help reduce their child's suffering? Compare this to a drug dealer who knowingly profits off the misery and addictions of others. These two cases are totally different, and call for different minimum sentencing guidelines. In America we have some of the best-trained criminal court judges in the world. We should trust them to use their judgment and discretion in cases like these, and not rely on mandatory minimum sentencing laws. Furthermore, a side effect of such laws is an ever-expanding prison population. This takes yet more taxpayer money away from schools, community programs and other initiatives in order to fund prisons.

policies.label: Allow enhanced interrogation
policies.text: Allow the military to use enhanced interrogation techniques, such as waterboarding, to gain information from suspected terrorists
policies.message_in_favor: While many techniques of enhanced interrogation should be banned, not all the techniques should be. For example, a common argument against enhanced interrogation is that it does not produce accurate intelligence that protects human lives. However, a 2015 report by the CIA concluded that enhanced interrogation has provided accurate intelligence, and is a key reason why Al-Qaeda has failed to launch a high-casualty attack in the West since 9/11. Therefore, instead of banning all techniques, some should be allowed but they should receive transparent evaluation and strict regulation. No one claims that there are not hard moral trade-offs in using these techniques; there is no easy answer when trading off the rights of suspected terrorists against the rights of citizens to not be bombed and maimed while going about their daily lives. However, on balance, banning all enhanced interrogation techniques is perhaps not in the interests of maximizing human welfare.
policies.message_against: Evidence shows that enhanced interrogation techniques are simply not effective. Therefore, they should not be allowed. In 2014, the U.S. Senate published a 525-page report into the CIA's enhanced interrogation program. It found that enhanced interrogation techniques did not produce reliable intelligence, nor gain cooperation from suspects. It also found the CIA's justification for using the techniques relied on bad evidence. For example, information that led to Osama bin Laden was reportedly obtained through standard techniques, and suspects who were subjected to enhanced interrogation techniques in fact tried to provide false and misleading information about bin Laden's whereabouts. Ultimately, while such techniques may occasionally provide useful information, evidence suggests this is rarely the case. The question then becomes: is it worth violating international law by torturing people — who are effectively innocent until proven guilty by a jury — for mainly useless information? The answer is No. America is better than that.

policies.label: Allow affirmative action
policies.text: Allow the use of affirmative action programs
policies.message_in_favor: Affirmative action can represent the American dream: no matter where you start in life, if you are provided with the opportunity then you can better yourself. For example, low-income students have historically been underrepresented at elite colleges in America. Many argue that this is because of 'legacy' admissions: students from wealthy families with connections who get admitted even if their grades are not up to scratch. At Harvard, for instance, acceptance rates for legacy students are about 33 percent, compared with an overall acceptance rate of 6 percent. Affirmative action in college admissions can help to correct this bias by increasing the number of low-income students who get admitted. Some people worry that such students would not be able to cope with the demands of elite college — but this is just not true. Research has shown that once admitted to top-tier colleges, low-income students complete their degree at higher rates and earn almost as much as wealthy students after graduation. This is the American dream in action, and it can be made possible by affirmative action programs.
policies.message_against: Affirmative action does not get to the root of discrimination and can actually backfire and hurt minority groups. For example, affirmative action in education can result in low-income students being admitted into colleges for which they are not prepared as their peers. This can happen because wealthy students are able to afford tutors during high school, but many low-income students cannot. As a result, some low-income students admitted to elite colleges find it hard to complete. This only serves to confirm stereotypes and demoralize low-income students. Evidence supports these concerns: when UCLA banned affirmative action in 1998, enrollment of black and Hispanic students dropped. However, the total number of black and Hispanic students graduating remained at a similar level as before the ban. This suggests that the minority students still being admitted were better matched to their peers, and that the college reduced failure rates for others by admitting fewer mismatched students. Therefore, instead of affirmative action, policy should focus on addressing disparities in wealth and opportunity earlier in the system.

policies.label: Increase capital gains tax
policies.text: Increase the government tax rate on profits earned from the sale of stocks, bonds, and real estate
policies.message_in_favor: This policy would mainly affect the mega-rich elite, and help level the playing field for ordinary hard-working Americans. Tax on profits earned from the sale of stocks, bonds and real estate is known as 'capital gains tax'. For the wealthiest elites in America, capital gains tax is often much less than federal income tax. As a result, middle-class American workers making $45,000 per year are taxed at a higher rate on their income (22% tax) than when some of the richest Americans — Bezos, Zuckerberg, Gates, Buffet — cash out a few billion dollars (20% tax). Is this right? No one likes being taxed. But taxes should be fair and proportionate. The wealthy elites make huge earnings off selling their stocks, bonds and real estate. Therefore, they are effectively being taxed less than the typical middle-class worker is for their earnings. The tax on stocks, bonds and real estate should be increased to match the income tax of ordinary hard-working Americans. That's only fair.
policies.message_against: This policy would mostly harm marginalized and low-income groups. Investing in stocks, bonds and real estate has been an effective method for generating wealth throughout history. The internet and smartphones have made it easier for all Americans to access these types of investments; allowing those traditionally excluded groups who were participating — such as low-income Americans — to now take part and generate wealth for themselves. Raising the tax rate on profits from these types of investments simply raises additional barriers for these traditionally-excluded groups to make profits that could change their lives. In contrast, wealthy elites would barely notice the increased tax rate and just carry on as normal. It is a coincidence that just as ordinary Americans are able to participate in a fair money-making market, there is a proposed tax hike that will make it harder for them? Unlikely. We should not increase the tax.

policies.label: Military aid to Saudi Arabia
policies.text: Provide U.S. military aid to Saudi Arabia during its conflict with Yemen
policies.message_in_favor: The civil war in Yemen directly harms Saudi Arabia's citizens, and the U.S. should support their safety and its longtime ally. After overthrowing the internationally-recognized Yemeni government, the Yemeni rebel movement has reportedly launched missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabian cities, used banned landmines, recruited children into their ranks, and fired artillery into populated areas — killing many civilians and blocking humanitarian aid access. Saudi Arabia is clearly not a perfect country nor ally, but they have been crucial in countering terrorist and Iranian aggression against American citizens. The U.S. should honor its international commitments by coming to their aid. Providing military aid to Saudi Arabia should also shorten the duration of the conflict — therefore reducing total casualties — because American military equipment is more advanced and precise.
policies.message_against: Saudi Arabia has repeatedly broken international law. As a world-leading democracy, the U.S. should send a strong signal that such violations will not be tolerated. For example, The Human Rights Watch has recorded unlawful Saudi-led coalition airstrikes, including deliberate attacks on civilians, with over 20,000 airstrikes bombing hospitals, school buses and markets. Therefore, over 17,500 civilians have been killed in Yemen, and a quarter of those who have died in the airstrikes are women and children. American-made missiles have been used to commit many of these atrocities, and the worst thing is that the U.S. has even further U.S. interests in the Middle East: the attacks are not to prevent the rise of a regional dominating political state (like ISIS); they are not designed to protect the global oil supply; and they do nothing to eliminate terrorists who directly threaten America. The U.S. shouldn't fight other country's wars just for the sake of it.

policies.label: Decrease power of labor unions
policies.text: Decrease the power of labor unions to help the economy
policies.message_in_favor: This policy is supported by expert economists and large research studies that suggest unions can be bad for the economy. For example, economist George Reisman concludes that, 'with few exceptions, unions openly combat the rise in the productivity of labor'. In addition, large research studies suggest that unions hurt profit and investment. A recent analysis of over 300 individual studies found that unionization can make businesses less profitable; and, by reducing profitability, unions can also discourage future investment in the business. Union disruption can be especially bad for businesses when the union is corrupt, as has been documented in many cases. Indeed, a closed culture can result in union members protecting each other from scrutiny and covering up union misconduct. This is especially problematic at police unions, which have been accused of permitting officers to abuse (primarily marginalized) citizens, and blocking reforms to prevent such abuse.
policies.message_against: Whether you generally like unions or not, the key question for the policy is whether unions hurt the economy. And there is powerful evidence they do no such thing. American economists John DiNardo and David Lee analyzed data from more than 27,000 businesses that faced union-organizing attempts over an 18-year period in America. They found that unionization had little or no effect on business survival rates, over 1–18-year time periods. This is powerful evidence that unions do not adversely affect business, and thus the economy. Supporting this conclusion, a recent analysis of more than 300 individual studies on the economic impact of unions around the world concluded that unionization does not reduce productivity. Therefore, the evidence speaks in a clear voice: decreasing the power of unions would not help the economy. This policy is misguided.

policies.label: Decrease foreign aid
policies.text: Decrease U.S. foreign aid spending
policies.message_in_favor: Due to corruption and weak institutions, a significant portion of foreign aid is stolen by economic elites in the recipient countries. The money can therefore do little to help and may actually hurt the citizens of those countries. For example, research published in the American Economic Review reports that many countries that receive foreign aid have high levels of corruption, and that foreign aid is less effective in countries with corrupt and weak institutions. Recent research from the World Bank finds that foreign aid donations coincide with sharp increases in deposits in offshore bank accounts that are known for secrecy and private wealth management. This evidence suggests aid is being diverted to corrupt economic elites. Clearly we should try to provide financial assistance to the poorest people around the world. However, good intentions are not enough — we need effective policy. Foreign aid money may be better spent elsewhere. For example, in reducing America's carbon emissions. This would do more to help the poorest countries because climate change is predicted to hit them hardest.
policies.message_against: The question of whether to decrease foreign aid or not depends on its effectiveness: does evidence show that foreign aid actually works? The answer is Yes. For example, the Brookings Institute — a prominent U.S. public policy organization — reports that deaths from malaria have declined nearly 50 percent since the year 2000, saving almost 7 million lives. This was made possible in part by U.S. foreign aid. Furthermore, research studies consistently find that foreign aid causes economic growth in countries that receive it. This shows that foreign aid helps countries become self-sufficient in the long-run; meaning they would not need aid forever. This promises economic benefits for America, because improving the economies of allies creates opportunities for new and beneficial trade deals. Foreign aid also increases U.S. influence around the world. Given that less than 1% of the U.S. federal budget goes to foreign aid — and it provides all these benefits — decreasing aid is just bad policy.

policies.label: Privatization of veterans' healthcare
policies.text: Increase privatization of veterans' healthcare
policies.message_in_favor: Whether you support or oppose the U.S. military, everyone should want veterans to receive the best care possible — because many of them suffered life-long mental and physical injuries as a result of their service. The key question is: would privately-managed care serve them better? Yes, the evidence suggests it would. Research reports that veterans' current, non-private healthcare provider has been involved in 'scandals', 'controversies' and 'shortfalls' in care that have contributed to the deaths of many veterans. This conclusion has also been reached by other, independent assessments. Meanwhile, privatizing care for veterans could reportedly mean shorter waits, more choices and fewer requirements for co-pays. It could also mean access to a wider array of mental health and female-specific services. Even a slight increase in service quality could have huge benefits, because there are about 22 million veterans living in the U.S. Privately-managed healthcare for veterans would still be funded by the government. Therefore, this policy is not about ideology; it is about providing services that can best care for those in need.
policies.message_against: Privatization would not improve healthcare services for veterans. For example, there is evidence that healthcare quality is in fact better in veterans' current, non-private care option than in the private sector. A 2016 study found that men with a variety of problems including pneumonia and heart attacks were less likely to die when treated at a veteran facility versus a non-veterans' in. In 2019 found that wait times at veterans' non-private clinics were similar to those in the private sector; not worse, as is commonly claimed. Many veterans also appear happy with their current, non-private healthcare. A 2018 survey of veterans showed that almost 75 percent reported trusting their current healthcare provider. If the evidence shows healthcare is no better under private, and veterans are happy with the way things are, then what is the basis to say that veterans' healthcare should be privatized?

policies.label: Increase tariffs on Chinese imports
policies.text: Increase U.S. tariffs on imported products from China
policies.message_in_favor: Proponents of tariffs usually focus on their economic benefits. However, increasing tariffs on Chinese products also has a human motivation: work standards in China are much lower than in the U.S., and many Chinese workers have limited or no rights and protections. For example, investigations by China Labor Watch — an organization that documents working conditions in China — reveals serious workers' rights violations. These include inadequate fire safety, lack of protective equipment, absence of labor unions, and management who verbally abuse workers. Other findings include a worker who was 'so exhausted because of the high production targets every day, her body ached all over and she could not help but cry in the dormitories'. This may be why Chinese products are so cheap. Increasing tariffs on Chinese imports into the U.S. would make their products less desirable to American consumers by increasing their price. This would hit the profits of Chinese factories, and serve as a strong signal that standards must be raised before Chinese products can again flow freely into America.
policies.message_against: Tariffs on Chinese products do nothing to improve the American economy nor create American jobs. This claim is supported by many studies of the impact of recent tariffs in America. For example, a recent study found that by the end of 2018, existing U.S. tariffs had reduced real income by $1.4 billion per month in added tax, and cost U.S. consumers an additional $3.2 billion per month in added tax. A 2019 paper by Federal Reserve Board economists found that steel tariffs had actually reduced jobs in the manufacturing sector, not protected them. The loss was equal to about 75,000 jobs. As a result of such evidence, most economists believe the policy will be overall negative for America: a recent Reuters poll of 60 economists found that 80% of them believed the impact would be negative, while the remaining believed it would be neutral. None believed that increasing tariffs on Chinese products would benefit America.

policies.label: Decrease estate tax
policies.text: Decrease the current estate tax rate
policies.message_in_favor: While the estate tax should not be abolished altogether, the tax rate is currently too high and should be decreased. The estate tax is a tax on the estate of a person who has died, such as their property, before it can be passed to their family (e.g., children). The maximum tax rate is 40%, meaning that nearly half of a dead parent's qualifying dollars can be prevented from being passed down to their children. This tax rate is higher than the highest bracket of federal income tax. There are two reasons why such a high rate is bad policy. First, the person who has just died has already paid a full amount of income tax on the earnings. Why should they be taxed again at such a high rate before their children can rightfully receive it? Second, because many Americans perceive it to be unfair, the high tax rate leads people to avoid paying the tax via clever estate management. Therefore, the economic benefit of the tax is actually much less than intended, making it an ineffective tool for wealth redistribution. Decreasing the estate tax rate may actually make the tax more effective, because more people will pay it.
policies.message_against: The current estate tax rate aligns with America's core values of hard work. (The estate tax is a tax on the estate of a person who has died, such as their property, before the estate is inherited by their relatives.) For example, the Founding Fathers argued that Americans should be able to get to the top through earning their wealth — based on fair competition — not through unearned, inherited handouts. In fact, handouts go against the values of America because they discourage hard work. Furthermore, the estate tax only applies to estates worth $11 million or more, and therefore the tax only applies to very wealthy individuals. Decreasing the estate tax simply gives their wealthy relatives even more money, further letting them 'off the hook' of having to work a job like everyone else. The tax should be kept as it is. America stands for hard work and effort, not handouts.

policies.label: Private pensions for public workers
policies.text: Transition pension plans for federal, state, and local government workers into privately managed accounts
policies.message_in_favor: We need a pension system that enables retired government workers to have a decent standard of living in their retirement. Privately-managed accounts would help achieve this because they generate higher returns than current public pensions. Current public pension investments return an average of 2.9% annually. By comparison, the average return of investments on the stock market is 7%. Therefore, Americans could potentially earn a lot more for their retirement through privately-managed accounts. And they could do so without accepting additional risk: the S&P 500 has never posted a loss over a 20-year rolling period. We should put aside ideology about privatization and focus on the most effective policy for helping public sector workers in their retirement. Evidence suggests that privatization is the right approach.
policies.message_against: This policy would cause a big debt problem for the federal government, and also does nothing to solve the current issues with Social Security. For example, currently the government uses the cash it receives from interest on Social Security pensions to fund various programs. Privatizing these pensions would cut this money off, meaning the government may have to borrow money from elsewhere, or raise taxes on citizens to make up for the losses. In addition, it is well known that Social Security is currently paying out more in benefits than it collects in revenue. Unless something is done, Social Security funds will be exhausted by 2034. Privatization will do nothing to stop this trend. That's why privatization of public pensions has failed to become law in past U.S. administrations. We need to put aside ideology and focus on what works to solve the problems we face; in this case, privatization is not the answer.
